problemStatement.formal:
Let $k\geq 2$ and $q(n,k)$ denote the least prime which does not divide $\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(n+i)$. Is it true that, if $k$ is fixed and $n$ is sufficiently large, we have\[q(n,k)<(1+o(1))\log n?\]



A problem of Erd\H{o}s and Pomerance.

The bound $q(n,k)<(1+o(1))k\log n$ is easy. It may be true this improved bound holds even up to $k=o(\log n)$.

A heuristic argument in favour of this is provided by Tao in the comments.

See also [457].

whyMatters: The least prime missing from a block of consecutive integers measures how completely short intervals cover small prime divisors.
The formalization turns the missing-prime function into a concrete Nat.find object with prime, nondivisibility, and minimality properties.
It connects elementary product divisibility to the sharper asymptotic Erdos-Pomerance prediction.

proven: There exists a prime that does not divide the product of k consecutive shifted terms, using infinitude of primes.
The smallestMissingPrime function is defined by Nat.find and proved prime, nondividing, and least among such primes.
Small primes p <= k divide the consecutive product, so the smallest missing prime is greater than k (Lean: q_gt_k).
The main-implies-weak bridge and monotonicity scaffolding are formalized without axioms.
open: The main Erdos-Pomerance conjecture remains open: for fixed k and large n, q(n,k) < (1 + o(1)) log n.
The easier bound q(n,k) < (1 + o(1)) k log n is noted but not proved in this file.
The possible extension to k = o(log n) remains heuristic/open.
